notice: See how each tradition says the same word.
description: One static page per pronunciation rule; examples come from the lookup data (most frequent words that show the rule, one per first letter).

pages.title: Kamatz (אָ)
pages.summary: The T-shaped vowel sign under a letter. Israeli and Sephardi readers say [a], like the a in "father". The Ashkenazi reading says [ɔ], like the o in "saw", so בָּרוּךְ is barukh in one and borukh in the other.
pages.who: Rule-generated: the [a] reading is the one used here for Israeli and Sephardi, the [ɔ] reading for Ashkenazi (the rule is "kamatz gadol is generally [ɔ]" in the cited description of Ashkenazi Hebrew). Not checked by a native speaker.
pages.limits: A few words use a kamatz that is read as a short o in every tradition (kamatz katan, as in כָּל "kol"). Only a short list of such words is recognised here, so other words of that kind are read wrongly.
pages.why: Kamatz (ָ): a in Israeli and Sephardi, but [ɔ] ("o" as in "saw") in Ashkenazi.

pages.title: Tav without a dot (ת)
pages.summary: A tav with no dagesh dot is t in the Israeli and Sephardi readings. In the Ashkenazi reading it is s, which is why שַׁבָּת is shabat in one and shabos in the other. A tav with a dot is t in all three.
pages.who: Rule-generated: Ashkenazi s for a tav without dagesh, as in the cited description ("ungeminated tav is pronounced [s]"). Some Sephardi communities say th or d here; those are not generated.
pages.limits: The rule needs the dagesh to be written in the pointed text. A word with the dot missing is read with s in the Ashkenazi column.
pages.why: Tav without a dagesh (ת): t in Israeli and Sephardi, but s in Ashkenazi (shabat / shabos).

pages.title: Holam (אֹ)
pages.summary: The dot above a letter. Israeli and Sephardi readers say a plain o. The Ashkenazi reading used here says "oy" [oj], the Polish and Galician value, so תּוֹרָה is torah in one and toyreh in the other.
pages.who: Rule-generated: one Ashkenazi value is chosen. Other Ashkenazi communities say o, ey or au; they are not shown. Not checked by a native speaker.
pages.limits: Only the Polish-style value is generated, so a reader from another Ashkenazi tradition will disagree with the Ashkenazi column.
pages.why: Cholam (ֹ): o in Israeli and Sephardi, but "oy" [oj] in the Polish-style Ashkenazi reading used here (other Ashkenazi readings differ and are not shown).

pages.title: Het (ח)
pages.summary: Israeli readers say [χ], a rasp at the back of the mouth, the same as khaf. The Sephardi reading used here is a deeper throat sound [ħ]. The Ashkenazi reading is [x], like khaf.
pages.who: Rule-generated from the cited tables. In practice many Ashkenazi and Sephardi readers say het and khaf alike, and some Sephardi and Mizrahi readers keep the throat sound.
pages.limits: The difference between [χ] and [x] is too small to hear in most voices; the [ħ] is the audible one.
pages.why: Het (ח): [χ] in Israeli, a deeper throat sound [ħ] in Sephardi, [x] in Ashkenazi.

pages.title: Ayin (ע)
pages.summary: Israeli and Ashkenazi readers say nothing for an ayin (it behaves like alef). The Sephardi reading used here keeps a throat sound [ʕ], a squeezed "ah" from deep in the throat.
pages.who: Rule-generated: [ʕ] for Sephardi follows the cited description. Spanish-Portuguese communities use a different sound [ŋ] that is not generated.
pages.limits: A silent ayin still splits the syllables, which the spelled-out respelling shows as an apostrophe.
pages.why: Ayin (ע): silent in Israeli and Ashkenazi, a throat sound [ʕ] in Sephardi.

pages.title: Resh (ר)
pages.summary: Israeli readers say a back-of-the-throat [ʁ], like the French r. The Sephardi and Ashkenazi readings used here say a front r, rolled or tapped like the Spanish r.
pages.who: Rule-generated: the Sephardi value follows the cited description. The Ashkenazi value is chosen from "alveolar flap or trill, or uvular by region"; a uvular Ashkenazi reader will disagree.
pages.limits: The respelling writes r for all three, so only the IPA line shows this difference.
pages.why: Resh (ר): a back-of-the-throat [ʁ] in Israeli, a front rolled or tapped r in Sephardi and Ashkenazi.

pages.title: Which syllable is stressed
pages.summary: Israeli and Sephardi readers stress the last syllable of most words (שַׁבָּת is sha-BAT). The Ashkenazi reading stresses the next-to-last syllable (SHA-bes). Some words are stressed earlier in every tradition, such as מֶלֶךְ (ME-lekh).
pages.who: Rule-generated: last-syllable stress is the default and exceptions come only from short existing lists; next-to-last stress is the default for Ashkenazi. Not checked by a native speaker.
pages.limits: About 240 words that look like two-syllable nouns ending in segol are read with last-syllable stress by default and may be wrong. Prefixed words (וּבְכָל) get an Ashkenazi stress a trained reader would not give.
